opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's changed quite a lot.

When I was younger, especially during the math competition years and then in undergrad, a big part of the reward was honestly external. You solve a hard problem, you get a medal, a professor notices you, you get into the program you wanted. There's a scoreboard, and doing difficult things was partly a way to prove to myself, and maybe to others, that I belonged in the room.

Then in research it started to shift. A real research problem doesn't come with an answer key. You can spend months on something and it doesn't work, and nobody is handing out points for the attempts. So the reward had to move inward. It became the moment when a structure suddenly makes sense, when you see why something is true, not just that it's true. That feeling is very quiet. Nobody else is in the room, but it's incredibly satisfying.

In the last couple of years, building a company, it changed again. Now the difficult things aren't only intellectual. Recruiting someone you really admire, convincing people that a direction is worth betting on, keeping a team motivated when an experiment fails. The reward there is more collective. When the team hits something we thought was maybe impossible six months earlier, and everyone feels it together, that's a different kind of joy from solving a problem alone at 2 a.m.

So I'd say it went from external validation, to private understanding, to shared progress. And maybe the deepest shift is that I care less now about whether the difficulty makes me look capable, and more about whether the thing is worth doing at all. If the problem matters, the difficulty is just the price of admission. I've come to almost enjoy that, because if it were easy, someone would have already done it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts early rewards like medals and recognition with the later satisfaction of understanding why a research result is true, and summarizes the shift as external validation to private understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's shifted from external validation to something much more internal, and honestly, much more about the people around me.

When I was younger, a lot of the reward came from recognition. Winning a competition, getting into a certain school, getting a prize. Those things are legible. You can point at them and say, "I did that." And I don't want to pretend that didn't matter to me. It did. It was motivating in a very real way.

But as I've gotten older, and especially since starting a company, I've noticed that those external markers stopped feeling like the thing itself. They started feeling like a lagging indicator of something else. What actually gives me energy now is the moment where something that seemed impossible becomes concrete. In math, it's when you finally see why a proof works and it becomes almost obvious in hindsight. In building a company, it's when you've been stuck on a problem for weeks and then a small group of people figure it out together, and you can feel the whole room's understanding shift at the same time.

That second part, the "together," is the biggest change. Doing hard things alone has a certain purity to it, but I've found that the reward is much deeper when it's shared. When a teammate comes back with a result you didn't expect, or when someone on the team grows into a problem that was over their head six months ago, that feels more meaningful to me than any individual achievement I've had.

And I think the other change is that I've become more comfortable with the reward being delayed, or even uncertain. When you're working on something genuinely hard, you don't get constant positive feedback. Most days feel like you're not making progress. So I've had to learn to find reward in the process itself: in the quality of the questions we're asking, in the fact that we're being honest about what we don't know. If you can't find some satisfaction there, you won't last long enough to see the outcome.

So, in short: less about being seen doing hard things, more about the hard things being real, and more about who I'm doing them with.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving away from recognition and external validation toward satisfaction in solving difficult problems and the work process itself, while also valuing doing that work with others.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s shifted from wanting to prove that I could do something difficult to asking whether the thing itself matters to me. Earlier, a lot of the reward came from reaching a milestone—there was a clear finish line, and getting there felt validating.

Now I find more satisfaction in the process of understanding something that initially felt out of reach. You can spend a long time feeling stuck, but then your questions get sharper, or you see a connection you couldn’t see before. I’ve come to appreciate those smaller changes more.

I still care about outcomes. But I’m less drawn to difficulty for its own sake. I want to feel that even if the outcome is uncertain, the work is worth spending my time on.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from proving capability and milestone validation toward valuing the process and whether the work matters personally. It does not clearly say the reward shifted from other people to the difficult work itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become less attached to the moment of proving that I can do something difficult. Earlier, a lot of the reward came from getting the answer or reaching a milestone—having that external confirmation that I’d done well. These days, I find more satisfaction in the process: staying with a problem when I don’t understand it yet, noticing that my thinking has changed, or working through something with people I enjoy learning from.

The outcome still matters to me. But I’m increasingly asking, “Is this something I actually care about?” rather than, “Would it be impressive if I succeeded?” That makes the difficulty feel more worthwhile, even when progress is slow.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier reward from external confirmation and impressive milestones with current satisfaction in staying with difficult problems and the learning process.
